title: Booster Lab: A Data-Centric Pipeline for Learning Deployable Humanoid Locomotion Policies
summary: Humanoid robot motion learning requires not only task-oriented control policies but also physically feasible and natural behaviors that can be transferred to real robots. However, robot-feasible motion data are often scarce: raw human demonstrations may be incompatible with the robot morphology, open-source clips vary in quality, and simulation-collected robot trajectories still require feasibility checking. To address these challenges, we propose a data-centric training and deployment pipeline that integrates motion data curation, real-to-sim model adaptation, AMP-based reinforcement learning, and sim-to-real deployment. We validate the framework on the Booster T1 robot and further provide preliminary cross-platform validation on Booster K1.

AI.tldr: A data-centric pipeline integrating motion data curation, real-to-sim adaptation, AMP-based reinforcement learning, and sim-to-real deployment for humanoid robot motion learning, validated on Booster T1 with preliminary cross-platform testing on K1.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robot motion learning requires both task-oriented control policies and physically feasible, natural behaviors, but robot-feasible motion data is scarce due to incompatibility between raw human demonstrations and robot morphology, variable quality of open-source clips, and the need for feasibility checking in simulation-collected trajectories.
AI.method: The proposed framework comprises four integrated components: (1) motion data curation, (2) real-to-sim model adaptation, (3) AMP-based reinforcement learning, and (4) sim-to-real deployment.
AI.result: The framework is validated on the Booster T1 robot and further provides preliminary cross-platform validation on the Booster K1.
AI.conclusion: The data-centric training and deployment pipeline successfully addresses the challenge of scarce robot-feasible motion data and enables effective motion learning for humanoid robots with physically feasible and natural behaviors.

title: PPO-EAL: Exact Augmented Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization for Safe Robotic Control
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising solution to accomplish complex robotic control tasks; however, most of the current work ignores the safety requirements. Safe RL seeks to maximize task performance while satisfying explicit physical constraints, but current algorithms struggle to learn the policy efficiently with precise constraint satisfaction. This work proposes PPO-EAL, a novel first-order constrained policy optimization framework that integrates exact augmented Lagrangian optimization into proximal policy optimization for safe robotic control. By combining clipped policy updates with exact quadratic penalty terms, PPO-EAL achieves theoretically grounded constraint enforcement without requiring impractically large penalty factors. A momentum-regulated multiplier update further improves dual-variable stability, reducing constraint oscillation and unsafe behavior while preserving task performance. We provide exactness and convergence analysis under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Extensive validation across diverse GPU-accelerated robotic benchmarks-including cart-pole balancing, cart-double-pendulum stabilization, 7-DoF Franka end-effector reaching, and quadrupedal locomotion-demonstrates superior safety precision and reward performance compared with state-of-the-art first-order safe RL baselines. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real deployment in a contact-rich gear assembly task, where PPO-EAL substantially improves task success, reduces peak contact force, and enhances operational robustness. These results establish PPO-EAL as a general and practically deployable safe RL framework for diverse safety-critical robotic systems.

AI.tldr: PPO-EAL integrates exact augmented Lagrangian optimization with proximal policy optimization to enable safe robotic control with precise constraint satisfaction, demonstrated across multiple benchmarks including sim-to-real deployment.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning is promising for robotic control but typically ignores safety requirements. Current safe RL algorithms struggle to learn policies efficiently while satisfying explicit physical constraints precisely.
AI.method: PPO-EAL combines clipped policy updates with exact quadratic penalty terms and momentum-regulated multiplier updates to integrate exact augmented Lagrangian optimization into proximal policy optimization, providing theoretically grounded constraint enforcement.
AI.result: Achieves superior safety precision and reward performance compared to state-of-the-art first-order safe RL baselines across diverse benchmarks (cart-pole, cart-double-pendulum, Franka reaching, quadrupedal locomotion). Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real deployment in gear assembly with improved success, reduced peak contact force, and enhanced operational robustness.
AI.conclusion: PPO-EAL establishes a general and practically deployable safe RL framework suitable for diverse safety-critical robotic systems.

title: LocalNav: Distilling Frontier VLMs and Embodied RL for On-Device Object Goal Navigation
summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have emerged in the robotic domain as a powerful tool that enables environmental perception with language context, serving as a catalyst for open-vocabulary tasks like ObjectNav. Yet, their computational footprint typically confines them to cloud execution, hindering low-latency inference with local deployment on resource-constrained robots. To address this challenge, we present a distillation strategy that transfers complex spatial-semantic reasoning from large frontier models into a lightweight, 4B-parameter local VLM for edge execution on embedded GPU devices (e.g., Jetson Orin). We first establish a State of the Art (SotA), Scene Graph (SG)-based pipeline using Claude Sonnet 4.6, achieving a 39.7% Success Rate (SR) on the HM3D OVON benchmark. We then demonstrate that fine-tuning Qwen3.5-4B on just 500 frontier reasoning traces effectively enables navigation capabilities, yielding a SR of 34.5%, narrowing the gap to the performance of large cloud models. Finally, we introduce E-RLVR with Token Generation (TG) regularization to compress output sequence lengths for physical deployment while grounding the agent in its task. This downstream optimization reduces TG overhead by 72.1% and latency by 71.8%. Combined with quantization, this joint strategy yields a cumulative 82.8% reduction in overall inference latency without significantly sacrificing performance, presenting a viable paradigm for local, low-latency VLM execution on mobile robots.

AI.tldr: A distillation strategy that transfers spatial-semantic reasoning from large frontier models to a lightweight 4B-parameter local VLM for edge execution, combined with token generation regularization and quantization to achieve 82.8% latency reduction without performance degradation.
AI.motivation: VLMs enable powerful environmental perception with language context for robotic tasks like ObjectNav, but their computational footprint typically confines them to cloud execution, hindering low-latency inference with local deployment on resource-constrained robots.
AI.method: 1) Established a SotA Scene Graph (SG)-based pipeline using Claude Sonnet 4.6; 2) Fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B on just 500 frontier reasoning traces; 3) Introduced E-RLVR with Token Generation (TG) regularization to compress output sequence lengths; 4) Combined with quantization.
AI.result: SG-based pipeline achieved 39.7% SR on HM3D OVON benchmark; fine-tuned Qwen3.5-4B achieved 34.5% SR (narrowing gap to large cloud models); TG overhead reduced by 72.1% and latency by 71.8%; combined with quantization, achieved 82.8% overall inference latency reduction without significant performance sacrifice.
AI.conclusion: This joint strategy presents a viable paradigm for local, low-latency VLM execution on mobile robots, enabling edge deployment while maintaining performance on resource-constrained embedded GPU devices like Jetson Orin.

title: S$^2$-VLA: State-Space Guided Vision-Language-Action Models for Long-Horizon Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in robotic manipulation, but their performance degrades significantly in long-horizon tasks due to cumulative error propagation. This limitation largely arises from static feature fusion mechanisms that rely on fixed weights to combine visual, language, and action representations, preventing the model from adapting to different phases of task execution. To address this limitation, we propose S$^2$-VLA, a framework that introduces a State-Space Guided Adaptive Attention (SSGAA) mechanism. SSGAA maintains a belief state that tracks task progression and generates dynamic gating weights to adaptively fuse information from three complementary sources visual features for spatial perception, task intents for high-level task planning, and temporal action sequences for execution consistency. This adaptive fusion allows the model to shift its focus throughout task execution, aligning with the evolving requirements of different task stages. Despite its compact 2B parameter size, S$^2$-VLA consistently outperforms larger 7B-scale models and achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon manipulation benchmarks, including LIBERO and SimplerEnv. highlighting the importance of adaptive feature fusion for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

AI.tldr: S²-VLA is a compact 2B parameter framework with State-Space Guided Adaptive Attention (SSGAA) that dynamically fuses visual, language, and action representations based on task progression to improve long-horizon robotic manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: VLA models degrade in long-horizon tasks due to static feature fusion mechanisms using fixed weights, preventing adaptation to different task execution phases.
AI.method: Introduces State-Space Guided Adaptive Attention (SSGAA) mechanism that maintains a belief state tracking task progression and generates dynamic gating weights to adaptively fuse visual features (spatial perception), task intents (high-level planning), and temporal action sequences (execution consistency).
AI.result: Despite being only 2B parameters, S²-VLA consistently outperforms larger 7B-scale models and achieves state-of-the-art performance on LIBERO and SimplerEnv long-horizon manipulation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive feature fusion is critical for long-horizon robotic manipulation, demonstrating that compact models with dynamic fusion mechanisms can outperform larger models with static fusion.

title: Swarm sign language: motion-based communication between drones
summary: In stealth-constrained swarm robotics, visual communication provides a critical alternative to active radio transmissions, which might be jammed. This research investigates motion-based communication for non-active information exchange, utilizing modular, dynamically feasible planar trajectories as visual cues. On the receiver drone end, a pose estimator tracks the transmitting drone's pose, feeding it into our custom 3DTrajDecoder. The decoder is designed to classify and segment the spatiotemporal sequence while simultaneously regressing its size and normal vector. To robustly train the decoder on both communicative and non-communicative trajectories, we developed a configurable online procedural generation pipeline. We validate our system through real-world testing and simulation to define its operating domain, supported by an extensive ablation study detailing our architectural choices and system limitations.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates motion-based visual communication for stealth-constrained swarm robotics, using modular planar trajectories as visual cues and a custom 3DTrajDecoder for pose estimation and trajectory classification.
AI.motivation: In stealth-constrained swarm robotics, visual communication provides a critical alternative to active radio transmissions, which might be jammed, enabling non-active information exchange.
AI.method: The research utilizes modular, dynamically feasible planar trajectories as visual cues. The receiver drone employs a pose estimator to track the transmitting drone's pose, which is fed into a custom 3DTrajDecoder that classifies and segments spatiotemporal sequences while regressing size and normal vector. A configurable online procedural generation pipeline was developed to train the decoder on both communicative and non-communicative trajectories.
AI.result: The system was validated through real-world testing and simulation to define its operating domain, supported by an extensive ablation study detailing architectural choices and system limitations.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a robust motion-based communication system for stealth-constrained swarm robotics that enables non-active information exchange through visual cues, with demonstrated validation through real-world testing and simulation.

title: Drifting in the Future: Stabilizing Path Following Drifting on High-Latency Vehicle Systems
summary: Autonomously controlling and handling a vehicle at and beyond its stability limit is a mathematically and computationally demanding task. Prior demonstrations of automated drifting have been limited to research platforms with instantaneous torque delivery and independently actuated wheels, leaving their applicability to production vehicles with actuator latencies and mechanically coupled axles uncertain. To overcome these issues, we design a predictor to compensate for powertrain delays, develop a revised control formulation to accommodate higher actuation latencies as well as a differential coupling on the driven axle, and introduce brake-based velocity stabilization. This paper presents the controller framework, the model extensions, and real-world experimental results. We observe that our controller enables a production sports car with a combustion engine to robustly sustain circular and figure-eight drifts, limiting lateral error to 1.1 m and sideslip overshoot to 0.06 rad despite actuator delays exceeding 250 ms, while mitigating oscillations and maintaining stable path and sideslip tracking. In conclusion, our results establish that autonomous drifting is feasible on production-ready vehicles, opening pathways to advanced safety systems capable of stabilizing cars in scenarios where traditional control fails.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a control framework for autonomous drifting on production vehicles by compensating for actuator delays and mechanical constraints, enabling a production sports car to sustain drifts with lateral error ≤1.1 m despite 250+ ms delays.
AI.motivation: Prior autonomous drifting demonstrations were limited to research platforms with instantaneous torque delivery and independently actuated wheels, making their applicability to production vehicles with actuator latencies and mechanically coupled axles uncertain.
AI.method: The authors developed a predictor to compensate for powertrain delays, a revised control formulation accommodating higher actuation latencies and differential coupling on the driven axle, and brake-based velocity stabilization.
AI.result: The controller enables a production sports car with a combustion engine to robustly sustain circular and figure-eight drifts, limiting lateral error to 1.1 m and sideslip overshoot to 0.06 rad despite actuator delays exceeding 250 ms, while mitigating oscillations and maintaining stable path and sideslip tracking.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous drifting is feasible on production-ready vehicles, opening pathways to advanced safety systems capable of stabilizing cars in scenarios where traditional control fails.

title: When Multi-Robot Systems Meet Agentic AI:Towards Embodied Collective Intelligence
summary: Embodied AI is increasingly becoming agentic, shifting robots from perception--control pipelines towards closed-loop systems that can retrieve context, deliberate during execution, monitor feedback, and refine future behavior. In parallel, robotics research has also moved from single-robot autonomy towards multi-robot systems, driven by the need for wider sensing, distributed action, heterogeneous capabilities, and fault tolerance. As AI agents move from single-agent use towards multi-agent collaboration, robotics faces a parallel challenge: robot teams must move beyond sharing maps, task assignments, and datasets towards sharing the state produced by embodied agent loops. This article explores Embodied Collective Intelligence (ECI), a future multi-robot paradigm in which a robot team accumulates and uses world context, task progress, and skill experience as shared resources. Specifically, we first review how embodied AI is becoming agentic and how multi-robot cooperation has evolved. We then present Embodied Collective Intelligence through Co-Perception, Co-Action, and Co-Evolution. Finally, we use an illustrative navigation study to examine one concrete component of the concept: shared world-memory inheritance. The study shows that a newly added robot can benefit from merged team memory, but it is not intended as a full evaluation of the ECI framework. Taken together, the review and conceptual framework motivate Embodied Collective Intelligence as a direction for embodied multi-agent intelligence, while the case study grounds one measurable part of the concept.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Embodied Collective Intelligence (ECI), a multi-robot paradigm where robot teams share context, task progress, and skill experience as collective resources through co-perception, co-action, and co-evolution components.
AI.motivation: As embodied AI evolves from simple perception-control pipelines to agentic closed-loop systems and robotics shifts from single-robot to multi-robot autonomy, there's a growing need to move beyond sharing static resources (maps, tasks, datasets) toward sharing dynamic states produced by embodied agent loops. Multi-agent collaboration requires robot teams to accumulate and utilize world context, task progress, and skill experience as shared resources.
AI.method: The authors review the evolution of embodied AI toward agentic systems and multi-robot cooperation. They present Embodied Collective Intelligence (ECI) as a conceptual framework comprising three core components: Co-Perception, Co-Action, and Co-Evolution. A navigation study is conducted to examine one concrete aspect—shared world-memory inheritance—to demonstrate how newly added robots benefit from merged team memory.
AI.result: The study demonstrates that newly added robots can benefit from merged team memory, validating the concept of shared world-memory inheritance as a component of ECI. However, the authors clarify this is not a full evaluation of the entire ECI framework but serves as an illustrative case study grounding one measurable aspect of the concept.
AI.conclusion: Embodied Collective Intelligence is proposed as a promising direction for embodied multi-agent intelligence. The framework motivates future research by establishing a conceptual foundation, while the navigation case study provides empirical grounding for one component. This work bridges the gap between agentic embodied AI and multi-robot collaboration by proposing that robot teams should share and accumulate dynamic states rather than just static resources.

title: Building a Scalable, Reproducible, Evaluatable, and Closed-Loop Simulation Environment Foundation for Embodied Intelligence Cloud-Native Simulation Infrastructure for Embodied Intelligence Training, Evaluation, and Data Collection
summary:
This paper presents a cloud-native simulation infrastructure framework for embodied intelligence that supports large-scale training, standardized evaluation, and simulation-based data collection. The framework unifies simulation environment generation, task execution, trajectory collection, model evaluation, data management, and cloud services into a scalable and reproducible platform.
  To address the high cost, limited scalability, and poor reproducibility of real-world robotic data collection, the framework adopts cloud-native technologies including elastic resource scheduling, containerized simulation, unified data management, and service-oriented system design, enabling efficient large-scale simulation for multi-model and multi-task workloads.
  Built on a four-layer architecture, the framework provides standardized environment assets, automated task generation, trajectory collection, benchmark evaluation, and closed-loop data optimization. It further integrates representative systems including D-VLA, RL-VLA3, Sword, and Pre-VLA to support scalable simulation, dynamic scheduling, visual augmentation, and real-time data filtering.
  We argue that cloud-native simulation infrastructure provides a unified foundation for data generation, model training, standardized evaluation, and real-world deployment, and will play a key role in the future development of embodied intelligence.

AI.tldr: A cloud-native simulation infrastructure framework for embodied intelligence that unifies simulation environment generation, task execution, trajectory collection, model evaluation, data management, and cloud services into a scalable and reproducible platform for large-scale training and standardized evaluation.
AI.motivation: To address the high cost, limited scalability, and poor reproducibility of real-world robotic data collection.
AI.method: Adopts cloud-native technologies including elastic resource scheduling, containerized simulation, unified data management, and service-oriented system design. Built on a four-layer architecture providing standardized environment assets, automated task generation, trajectory collection, benchmark evaluation, and closed-loop data optimization.
AI.result: The framework successfully integrates with representative systems including D-VLA, RL-VLA3, Sword, and Pre-VLA to support scalable simulation, dynamic scheduling, visual augmentation, and real-time data filtering.
AI.conclusion: Cloud-native simulation infrastructure provides a unified foundation for data generation, model training, standardized evaluation, and real-world deployment, playing a key role in the future development of embodied intelligence.

title: Translation as a Bridging Action: Transferring Manipulation Skills from Humans to Robots
summary: We study whether we can learn novel manipulation skills from human actions to a bi-manual robot with parallel grippers. Human action data is cheap, abundant, and diverse, making it one of the most promising resources for scaling up robot learning. Yet transferring skills from humans to robots remains hard: most prior work treats humans as just another bi-manual 6DoF embodiment, where hand-pose estimates are noisy and the contact patterns of human fingers differ fundamentally from those of a parallel gripper. We argue that learning rotation-inclusive action signals from human data is therefore sub-optimal, and instead propose a bridging action representation: the relative wrist translation within the initial head-camera frame, an action space shared by humans and robots. To handle the potential absence of certain action components in different embodiments, we build a $π_0$-like vision-language-action model with interleaved action tokens and attention masking. On a suite of novel bi-manual manipulation tasks, our bridging action transfers human manipulation knowledge to robots far more effectively than noisy 6DoF human actions and scales with the amount of human data.

AI.tldr: The paper studies learning novel bi-manual manipulation skills from human actions for a robot with parallel grippers. Instead of using noisy 6DoF human hand poses, they propose a bridging action representation (relative wrist translation within the initial head-camera frame) shared by humans and robots, implemented via a π0-like vision-language-action model with interleaved action tokens and attention masking.
AI.motivation: Human action data is cheap, abundant, and diverse, making it a promising resource for scaling robot learning. However, transferring skills from humans to robots is challenging because most prior work treats humans as just another bi-manual 6DoF embodiment, where hand-pose estimates are noisy and human finger contact patterns differ fundamentally from parallel grippers. Learning rotation-inclusive action signals from human data is therefore sub-optimal.
AI.method: The authors propose a bridging action representation: relative wrist translation within the initial head-camera frame, an action space shared by humans and robots. They build a π0-like vision-language-action model with interleaved action tokens and attention masking to handle potential absence of certain action components in different embodiments.
AI.result: On a suite of novel bi-manual manipulation tasks, the bridging action representation transfers human manipulation knowledge to robots far more effectively than noisy 6DoF human actions. The method scales with the amount of human data available.
AI.conclusion: The bridging action representation effectively transfers human manipulation knowledge to robots for bi-manual manipulation tasks, overcoming limitations of using raw 6DoF human hand poses that suffer from noise and embodiment differences.

title: PA-BiCoop: A Primary-Auxiliary Cooperative Framework for General Bimanual Manipulation
summary: Bimanual manipulation is essential for advanced robotic systems because it offers higher efficiency and flexibility compared to single-arm configurations. However, existing approaches either lack inter-arm interaction or ignore the need for a dynamic division of labor, treating the arms as functionally equivalent. To address these limitations, this paper draws inspiration from human bimanual manipulation where one arm handles core operations and the other provides auxiliary support, and proposes PA-BiCoop, a new single-model bimanual cooperation framework with dynamic primary-auxiliary arm differentiation. PA-BiCoop categorizes robotic arms into primary and auxiliary arms with adaptively adjustable roles across task stages, employs two specialized decoders that share a global feature encoder: the primary decoder generates the primary arm's base-coordinate pose and core-task affordance heatmaps, and the auxiliary decoder outputs the auxiliary arm's relative pose in the primary arm's coordinate system. Moreover, we design a dynamic role assignment module to automatically map roles to left/right arms without manual pre-definition. This design facilitates inter-arm knowledge sharing and coordinated manipulation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our PA-BiCoop achieves superior performance: it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by 48% on average in RLBench2 simulation tasks and by over 50% on average in real world tasks, thereby verifying its effectiveness and advancement in bimanual manipulation.

AI.tldr: PA-BiCoop is a single-model bimanual cooperation framework that dynamically assigns primary and auxiliary roles to arms based on task stages, using shared encoders and specialized decoders to enable inter-arm knowledge sharing for superior manipulation performance.
AI.motivation: Existing bimanual manipulation approaches either lack inter-arm interaction or treat arms as functionally equivalent, ignoring the human-like dynamic division of labor where one arm handles core operations while the other provides auxiliary support.
AI.method: PA-BiCoop proposes a dynamic primary-auxiliary arm differentiation framework with: 1) Two specialized decoders sharing a global feature encoder, where the primary decoder generates base-coordinate pose and affordance heatmaps while the auxiliary decoder outputs relative pose; 2) A dynamic role assignment module that automatically maps roles to left/right arms without manual pre-definition.
AI.result: PA-BiCoop outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by 48% on average in RLBench2 simulation tasks and over 50% on average in real-world tasks, demonstrating significant improvements in bimanual manipulation performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PA-BiCoop framework effectively addresses the limitations of existing approaches by enabling dynamic arm role assignment and inter-arm knowledge sharing, achieving superior performance in both simulated and real-world bimanual manipulation tasks.

title: Learning Stable In-Grasp Manipulation in a Non-Dropping Action Space
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Traditionally, dexterous manipulation controllers are designed using analytic models constrained by strong assumptions about the hand and the objects being manipulated. Reinforcement learning (RL) has become another common approach in which skills are explored openly in an end-to-end manner but is inefficient because of unnoticeable instability and conflicts in learning objectives. This paper attempts to efficiently explore stable and accurate manipulation skills by decomposing dexterous skills into multiple simpler/analyzable components. Each skill component is subsequently learned with constraints and guidance from classical physics and control theory. Our work shows that for stable grasp, in-grasp reposition/reorientation with different objects, sensor/motor noise, latency, and frictional conditions, skill learning becomes efficient and stable with prior knowledge from theory.

AI.tldr: This paper decomposes dexterous manipulation skills into simpler, analyzable components and learns them with constraints and guidance from classical physics and control theory, achieving efficient and stable skill learning across various challenging scenarios.
AI.motivation: Traditional dexterous manipulation controllers rely on analytic models constrained by strong assumptions about hands and objects, while reinforcement learning (RL) explores skills end-to-end but suffers from inefficiency due to unnoticeable instability and conflicting learning objectives.
AI.method: The authors decompose dexterous skills into multiple simpler/analyzable components. Each skill component is learned with constraints and guidance from classical physics and control theory, combining the strengths of both approaches.
AI.result: Skill learning becomes efficient and stable when incorporating prior knowledge from theory across various challenging conditions: stable grasp, in-grasp reposition/reorientation with different objects, sensor/motor noise, latency, and varying frictional conditions.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging prior knowledge from classical physics and control theory enables more efficient and stable skill learning for dexterous manipulation, bridging the gap between model-based approaches and end-to-end reinforcement learning.

title: Unleashing Infinite Motion: Scaling Expressive Quadrupedal Motion via Generative Video Priors
summary: Quadruped robots have achieved remarkable locomotion, yet their behavioral repertoire remains confined to a few gaits--far from the expressive, companion-like presence long envisioned for them. Attempts to import the humanoid recipe of large-scale motion data have inherited one tacit assumption: that robot motion must first pass through an animal body, making data collection dependent on cooperative animals, reconstruction fragile across species, and retargeting ill-posed across incompatible morphologies. We propose Uni-Mo, a fully automated pipeline that removes the animal from the loop by reframing data scarcity as a generation problem: an LLM proposes motion prompts, a video diffusion model synthesizes the corresponding robot behaviors, and the generated videos are lifted into 3D reference trajectories used to train tracking policies deployed on a real Unitree Go2. To make naively-drifting generations reliably extractable, we introduce an Identity Consistency Loss that enforces appearance coherence across frames. We release Quad-Imaginarium at https://github.com/GaoLii/Quad-Imaginarium.git, the resulting open-source dataset of 7,488 language-annotated quadruped motions (18.5 hours) spanning acrobatic and performative behaviors. We validate 392 randomly sampled motions on a real Unitree Go2 with a 96.7% deployment success rate, complemented by a 97.6% success rate across the full dataset in simulation.

AI.tldr: Uni-Mo is a fully automated pipeline that generates quadruped robot motion data using LLMs and video diffusion models, eliminating the need for animal data collection. It introduces the Quad-Imaginarium dataset with 7,488 language-annotated motions (18.5 hours) and achieves 96.7% deployment success rate on real Unitree Go2 robots.
AI.motivation: Quadruped robots have limited behavioral repertoire despite remarkable locomotion capabilities. Existing approaches that import humanoid motion data require cooperative animals, suffer from fragile reconstruction across species, and face ill-posed retargeting across incompatible morphologies.
AI.method: Uni-Mo reframes data scarcity as a generation problem: an LLM proposes motion prompts, a video diffusion model synthesizes corresponding robot behaviors, and these are lifted into 3D reference trajectories for training tracking policies on real robots. The pipeline introduces an Identity Consistency Loss to enforce appearance coherence across frames.
AI.result: Released Quad-Imaginarium dataset containing 7,488 language-annotated quadruped motions spanning acrobatic and performative behaviors (18.5 hours). Validation shows 96.7% deployment success rate on real Unitree Go2 for 392 sampled motions and 97.6% success rate across the full dataset in simulation.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that fully automated motion generation for quadrupeds is feasible, overcoming traditional limitations of animal-based data collection. This approach enables more diverse behavioral capabilities for quadruped robots without requiring animal cooperation or species-specific reconstruction.

title: SimFoundry: Modular and Automated Scene Generation for Policy Learning and Evaluation
summary: Training and evaluating robot policies in the real world is costly and difficult to scale. We introduce SimFoundry, a modular and automated system for zero-shot real-to-sim scene construction from a video. SimFoundry generates sim-ready digital twins and supports object, scene, and task editing, enabling the automated generation of diverse digital cousins: affordance-preserving variations of reconstructed real-world scenes. Policies trained on SimFoundry data transfer zero-shot to challenging real tasks involving multi-step manipulation, articulated object interaction, and bimanual interaction, and its digital cousins (variations of the original scene, objects, and tasks) facilitate generalization to new real-world conditions. Across 7 manipulation tasks and 5 policy architectures, SimFoundry simulation evaluations strongly predict real-world performance, with mean Pearson correlation 0.911 and mean maximum ranking violation 0.018. When evaluating sim-trained policies zero-shot in the real world, policies trained with object, scene, and task cousins in simulation show average task success rate improvements of 17%, 21%, and 40%, respectively. Additional details at https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/simfoundry/ .

AI.tldr: SimFoundry is a modular system for zero-shot real-to-sim scene construction from videos, generating sim-ready digital twins and affordance-preserving variations (digital cousins) that enable zero-shot policy transfer and significant real-world generalization.
AI.motivation: Training and evaluating robot policies in the real world is costly and difficult to scale, creating a need for effective simulation-based approaches that can enable broader deployment.
AI.method: SimFoundry is a modular and automated system that performs zero-shot real-to-sim scene construction from videos, generating sim-ready digital twins and supporting object, scene, and task editing to create affordance-preserving variations (digital cousins) of reconstructed scenes.
AI.result: Across 7 manipulation tasks and 5 policy architectures, SimFoundry simulation evaluations strongly predict real-world performance (Pearson correlation 0.911, max ranking violation 0.018). Zero-shot real-world evaluation shows task success rate improvements of 17% with object cousins, 21% with scene cousins, and 40% with task cousins.
AI.conclusion: SimFoundry enables automated generation of diverse digital twins and cousins that facilitate zero-shot policy transfer to challenging real tasks (multi-step manipulation, articulated object interaction, bimanual interaction) and significantly improve real-world generalization, with strong correlation between simulation and real-world performance metrics.

title: CacheMPC: Certified Cached Model Predictive Control for Quadruped Locomotion
summary: Model Predictive Control (MPC) is the standard predictive layer in hierarchical quadruped controllers, but the per-cycle QP solve limits the update rate achievable on embedded processors. Because legged gaits revisit a bounded region of state space, MPC solutions admit caching and reuse. This paper proposes \emph{Certified CacheMPC}: a Locality-Sensitive-Hashed cache of horizon contact-force trajectories, partitioned by contact mode, retrieved at query time and accepted only when an a-posteriori per-query certificate confirms primal feasibility and a Lagrangian dual-gap upper bound on cost suboptimality. A bounded-budget controller schedule combines top-$K$ certified retrieval, a deadline-bounded QP solve, and a shifted last-certified fallback. The framework is evaluated on a Unitree Go2 across $2{,}038$ usable cold-controller MuJoCo trials, including a $600$-trial $n\!=\!50$ campaign at three failure-boundary cells, and a first-deploy session on the on-robot NVIDIA Orin NX. The un-gated cache delivers a $25\times$ median solve-time speedup in simulation and an $18.7\times$ median speedup on hardware. At $n\!=\!50$ no statistically significant difference in closed-loop stable rate is detected between the cache variants and the no-cache baseline at any tested cell. The certificate's contribution to closed-loop safety is not resolvable at the present sample size.

AI.tldr: Certified CacheMPC uses a locality-sensitive hashed cache of horizon contact-force trajectories with a-posteriori feasibility and optimality certificates, achieving 25× simulation and 18.7× hardware speedups over baseline MPC while maintaining comparable closed-loop stability at n=50.
AI.motivation: MPC is the standard predictive layer in hierarchical quadruped controllers, but per-cycle QP solve limits update rates on embedded processors. Legged gaits revisit bounded regions of state space, suggesting MPC solutions can be cached and reused.
AI.method: A Locality-Sensitive-Hashed cache partitions horizon contact-force trajectories by contact mode. At query time, cached solutions are retrieved and accepted only when an a-posteriori certificate confirms primal feasibility and provides a Lagrangian dual-gap upper bound on cost suboptimality. A bounded-budget controller schedule combines top-K certified retrieval, a deadline-bounded QP solve, and a shifted last-certified fallback.
AI.result: Evaluated on Unitree Go2 across 2,038 MuJoCo trials (including 600-trial n=50 campaign at failure-boundary cells) and on-robot NVIDIA Orin NX. Ungated cache delivers 25× median solve-time speedup in simulation and 18.7× on hardware. At n=50, no statistically significant difference in closed-loop stable rate between cache variants and no-cache baseline. Certificate's contribution to closed-loop safety not resolvable at present sample size.
AI.conclusion: Certified CacheMPC provides substantial computational efficiency gains while maintaining comparable closed-loop stability performance. The certification framework ensures safety through feasibility and optimality guarantees, though the quantifiable safety contribution requires larger sample sizes to determine.

title: WARP-RM: A Warp-Augmented Relative Progress Reward Model for Data Curation
summary: Scaling imitation learning requires large datasets, yet human teleoperation inevitably produces mixed-quality demonstrations containing hesitations and recoveries. Prior frame-level progress reward models supervise on absolute temporal progress proxies that suffer from label noise, or require costly human annotations to define subtask boundaries. We present WARP (Warp-Augmented Relative Progress), a novel fully self-supervised algorithm for learning dense, signed relative progress magnitudes directly from successful demonstrations. WARP generates per-frame progress targets via time-warp augmentations of demonstrations (variable playback speeds and reversals) and we train WARP-RM to predict the normalized elapsed time between input frames. Aggregating these predictions across overlapping windows yields a dense frame-level progress signal. We then introduce WARP-BC, which leverages these scalar reward estimates to upweight high-advantage action chunks during behavior cloning, where chunk-level advantage is obtained by aggregating per-frame rewards. We evaluate our approach on a physical bimanual robot system performing a long-horizon deformable object manipulation task: folding T-shirts from a random crumpled start. To evaluate policy robustness against suboptimal data, we construct training datasets of varying quality using episode length as a proxy for teleoperation sub-optimality. As the dataset is widened to admit more inefficiencies, WARP-BC maintains a 19/20 success rate compared to vanilla BC's collapse to 2/20, improving throughput by up to 18x.

AI.tldr: WARP (Warp-Augmented Relative Progress) is a self-supervised algorithm that learns dense relative progress signals from demonstrations via time-warp augmentations, enabling behavior cloning to maintain high performance (19/20 success) even with noisy, suboptimal teleoperation data, outperforming vanilla BC (2/20 success) by up to 18x throughput.
AI.motivation: Scaling imitation learning requires large datasets, but human teleoperation produces mixed-quality demonstrations with hesitations and recoveries. Prior frame-level progress reward models have limitations: they supervise on absolute temporal progress proxies that suffer from label noise, or require costly human annotations to define subtask boundaries.
AI.method: WARP generates per-frame progress targets through time-warp augmentations of demonstrations (variable playback speeds and reversals), training a progress reward model (WARP-RM) to predict normalized elapsed time between input frames. Aggregating these predictions across overlapping windows yields a dense frame-level progress signal. WARP-BC then leverages these scalar reward estimates to upweight high-advantage action chunks during behavior cloning, where chunk-level advantage is obtained by aggregating per-frame rewards.
AI.result: Evaluated on a physical bimanual robot performing T-shirt folding, with training datasets of varying quality constructed using episode length as a proxy for teleoperation sub-optimality. WARP-BC maintains a 19/20 success rate compared to vanilla BC's 2/20, and improves throughput by up to 18x.
AI.conclusion: WARP-BC demonstrates superior robustness against suboptimal data compared to vanilla behavior cloning. By learning dense relative progress signals in a fully self-supervised manner, the approach maintains high performance even as datasets include more inefficiencies, suggesting that self-supervised progress signals can effectively handle noisy human demonstrations.

title: DexCompose: Reusing Dexterous Policies for Multi-Task Manipulation with a Single Hand
summary: Dexterous manipulation policies can solve individual skills, but composing them to perform multiple tasks with a single hand remains challenging. Adding a new task on top of an existing manipulation skill often imposes conflicting demands on overlapping fingers and contact modes, causing destructive interference between preserving an existing manipulation outcome and executing a new one. We propose DexCompose, a role-aware residual composition framework that reuses pretrained dexterous policies for multi-task manipulation through explicit finger-level action ownership. Given two pretrained full-hand policies, DexCompose first collects successful post-task states from the first skill and performs release tests over candidate finger masks to identify which fingers are necessary for maintaining the established skill state. It then trains two asymmetric residual modules: a bounded residual stabilizer for task preservation, and a context-aware residual that adapts the frozen downstream policy only within the action subspace assigned to the new task. We evaluate the framework on 16 composite dexterous manipulation tasks spanning four object-retention skills and four downstream interactions. DexCompose achieves a 77.4% average composite success rate, demonstrating that structural action ownership with dual residuals offers a promising direction for composing dexterous skills beyond conventional policy chaining.

AI.tldr: DexCompose is a role-aware residual composition framework that enables multi-task dexterous manipulation by reusing pretrained policies through explicit finger-level action ownership and dual asymmetric residual modules, achieving 77.4% success rate on 16 composite tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing dexterous manipulation policies struggle to compose multiple tasks in a single hand because new tasks impose conflicting demands on overlapping fingers and contact modes, causing destructive interference with preserving established skill states.
AI.method: DexCompose collects successful post-task states from a pretrained skill, performs release tests on finger masks to identify necessary fingers, and trains two asymmetric residual modules: a bounded residual stabilizer for task preservation and a context-aware residual for adapting the frozen downstream policy within the action subspace assigned to the new task.
AI.result: Evaluated on 16 composite dexterous manipulation tasks spanning four object-retention skills and four downstream interactions, DexCompose achieves a 77.4% average composite success rate.
AI.conclusion: Structural action ownership with dual residuals demonstrates a promising direction for composing dexterous skills beyond conventional policy chaining, effectively resolving conflicts between preserving existing manipulation outcomes and executing new tasks.
